cues.text: Son of Zebedee
John was a fisherman of Galilee, son of Zebedee and Salome and younger brother of the Apostle James the Greater .
The two were mending their nets when Christ called them, and they left boat and father at once.
For their fiery temper the Lord surnamed the brothers Boanerges — sons of thunder.
From the first John belonged to the inner circle of three, present with Peter and James at the raising of Jairus's daughter, at the Transfiguration, and in the agony of Gethsemane.
The Beloved Disciple
In the Fourth Gospel John never names himself, referring to himself only as the disciple whom Jesus loved.
It is he who reclines next to the Lord at the Last Supper and asks who will betray him.
When the other Apostles had fled, the disciple whom Jesus loved is described as standing at the foot of the Cross beside the Mother of Jesus, where Jesus entrusted Mary to him: Behold thy mother.
From that hour, the Gospel says, the disciple took her to his own.
Witness of the Resurrection
On Easter morning, hearing Mary Magdalen 's report, John outran Peter to the empty tomb, and seeing the linen cloths laid in order, he believed.
By the Sea of Tiberias it was John who first recognized the risen Christ on the shore — It is the Lord — while Peter plunged into the water to reach him.
Through the Acts of the Apostles he appears at Peter's side, healing the lame man at the Temple gate and going to Samaria to confer the Holy Spirit.
The Evangelist and Theologian
To John the Church ascribes the Fourth Gospel , three Epistles, and the Book of Revelation.
His Gospel stands apart from the other three in its soaring theology, opening with the eternal Word who was with God and was God, and who was made flesh and dwelt among us.
So lofty is his vision that his symbol became the eagle, and Christian tradition gave him the title the Theologian .
His letters return again and again to a single theme, that God is love and that those who abide in love abide in God.
The Johannine Writings

The books ascribed to John form a world of their own within the New Testament, marked by a handful of luminous words repeated like themes in music — light and darkness , truth , life , and above all love .
Where the other Gospels recount many parables, John selects a few signs and draws out their meaning in long discourses: the bread of life, the good shepherd, the true vine.
Early witnesses, among them St. Irenaeus , who as a boy had heard Polycarp speak of the Apostle, testify that the beloved disciple stood behind the Johannine tradition.
That tradition was set down in the Gospel after the other evangelists, to confirm the Church in the divinity of Christ.
Patmos and Revelation
Ancient tradition places John's later ministry at Ephesus , where he governed the churches of Asia.
Under the persecution of Domitian he was exiled to the island of Patmos , and there received the visions recorded in the Apocalypse, the last book of the Bible.
It is a revelation of Christ in glory and of the Church's final triumph through tribulation.
Early writers relate that before his exile he was cast into a cauldron of boiling oil at Rome and came out unharmed.
Ephesus and Death
According to ancient Christian tradition, John was the only one of the Twelve believed not to have died a martyr.
He is traditionally said to have died at Ephesus in extreme old age, around the end of the first century.
St. Jerome preserves the memory that in his last days, too feeble to preach at length, he would repeat over and over the same words: Little children, love one another.
Asked why, he answered that it was the Lord's command, and if it alone were kept, it was enough.
His feast is kept on December 27 , within the octave of Christmas.
